claims.text: Engineered local surface electronic interactions enhance ethanol oxidation activity in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts.
A slight controlled oxidation preferentially changes the oxidation state of surface Rh.
Preferential oxidation of Rh produces electronic modulation between neighboring Pt and Rh sites.
Pt–Rh electronic modulation optimizes the adsorption and activation of ethanol and its intermediates.
The as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
The as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles have a random elemental distribution.
Mild oxidative pretreatment can partially oxidize surface Rh without significantly changing the bulk composition.
Selective mild oxidation of Rh creates a localized d-band change at neighboring Pt–Rh sites.
Oxidation shifts the local d-band center of Rh and thereby changes the electronic properties of adjacent Pt atoms.
The proposed electronic tuning lowers the activation energy for ethanol dehydrogenation.
The proposed electronic tuning produces balanced adsorption of ethanol oxidation intermediates.
Lower dehydrogenation barriers and balanced intermediate adsorption increase catalytic turnover.
The proposed electronic tuning may favor complete ethanol oxidation pathways.
The oxidatively pretreated catalyst will have higher ethanol oxidation current density than the untreated catalyst.
The oxidatively pretreated catalyst will show greater selectivity toward complete oxidation, including a higher CO2-to-partial-products ratio.
The oxidatively pretreated catalyst will be more durable during prolonged ethanol oxidation than the untreated catalyst.

The proposed mechanism applies to sub-10 nm solid-solution particles in alkaline electrolyte at 60–80°C under moderately oxidizing or reducing reaction conditions, provided particle size and structure remain intact.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply when reaction conditions cause substantial particle sintering or bulk phase changes.
Untreated as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles provide the experimental baseline.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in activity, complete-oxidation selectivity, or durability relative to the untreated control is specified as a falsifying result.
